context.guidance: Serialise only the fields a response needs, using explicit allow-lists or response shapes rather than whole models or nested records. Remove Personal Data Elements the requester is not entitled to see, so each response stays within the Purpose for which the data was collected under §6(1). Apply the same field limits on every route that returns the same record, as Rule 6(1)(b) requires for access control.

value.fix: Don't send the raw review documents. Map each review to an explicit allow-list of fields before you serialise it, and remove personal data such as the author's email and the likedBy array of user emails. For example: `const safe = reviews.map(r => ({ id: r._id, product: r.product, message: r.message, likesCount: Array.isArray(r.likedBy) ? r.likedBy.length : 0, liked: Array.isArray(r.likedBy) && req.user ? r.likedBy.includes(req.user.email) : false })); res.json(utils.queryResultToJson(safe))`. Use the same pattern in the database query too, with a projection such as `db.reviewsCollection.find({ product: id }, { projection: { author: 0, likedBy: 0 } })`, so the extra fields are never loaded. Only include the author when the requester is that author or an admin, for example `author: (req.user && (req.user.email === r.author || req.user.role === 'admin')) ? r.author : undefined`. Put this mapping in one shared helper, such as `toPublicReview(review, requester)`, and call it from every route that returns reviews (show, create, update, like and any admin or listing endpoints). That keeps the field limits the same on every route, in line with the access-control rule.
